what: Per-endpoint response KEY SETS for every grandfathered Class B.2 endpoint+method pair in
ALIGNMENT.md § 'Current Class B inventory', recorded from the wire by booting a real
server.mjs and probing it. Values are never recorded — only key paths, the HTTP status and
the content-type — so uptime, timestamps and counters cannot make this file flap.
This is the mechanism that replaced the ADR 0012 prose grep (#346). The grep could only ever
see additions whose author WROTE the marker; a field added with no marker produced 'none this
cycle', which is a green result for the exact case it was least able to see. This file is
produced from what the server actually returns, so it does not depend on anyone writing
anything. Its git history IS the per-release record of how B.2 surface grew:
TWO CONFIGURATION PROFILES, one block each (#357): `probes` is the default configuration every
production instance in the reference fleet runs, and `probesTuiPool` is the config-variant corner
with TUI mode, a warm pane pool and skip-permissions all ON. The single original profile left 12
key paths unrecorded, 10 of them inside /health's `tui.pool` — a TuiPanePool.stats() counter bag,
i.e. exactly where the next field is most likely to land. The profiles are defined in
scripts/b2-key-snapshot.mjs § B2_PROFILES; read that before adding a third.
Generated and checked by scripts/b2-key-snapshot.mjs. The suite fails on any difference.
Read notCovered below before treating a green run as coverage.
regenerate: node scripts/b2-key-snapshot.mjs --write   (then state the field names in the PR body AND the CHANGELOG — ADR 0012 condition 5)

keyPathNotation.a.b: object member b of object member a
keyPathNotation.a[]: a is an ARRAY; recorded even when empty, so array->object is visible
keyPathNotation.a[].b: member b of some element of array a (union over all elements)
keyPathNotation.present-but-null: IN the key set — /health's instanceName ships as "" rather than being omitted (#327) precisely so consumers can tell null from absent, and this preserves that

howToReadNotCovered: Every entry is tagged with HOW IT WAS ESTABLISHED, because that is the part a reader is
actually weighing when deciding whether to trust this file:
[measured]  observed from a running server.mjs, or from executing the code named in the entry
[reasoned]  derived from reading the implementation, not observed

[measured, except where marked]  the entry mixes claims established DIFFERENTLY and each is marked inline. Used when splitting the entry would separate a fact from the reason it matters. Read the inline marks; do not read the header tag as covering the whole entry.
This tagging exists because #354's review caught a REASONED claim recorded in the same
voice as a measured one, and it was wrong (the CLAUDE_TUI_MODE / tui.pool entry below).
A blind-spot note is read by someone deciding whether to trust the mechanism, so a note
that authoritatively points in the wrong direction is worse than a missing one: it spends
the credibility of 'we measured this' on a claim that was not measured.
notCovered: [measured] TYPE changes under an unchanged key path. A key set records names, not types: responseKeyPaths({a:'x'}) and responseKeyPaths({a:1}) are both ['a']. Container changes ARE visible (object <-> scalar adds/removes children; array <-> object adds/removes the '[]' marker).

[measured] RENAMES, as renames. Renaming 'old' to 'new' produces exactly '+ new' and '- old' from diffB2KeySets — the test fails, which is the point, but nothing in the output distinguishes a rename from an unrelated removal plus an unrelated addition.

[measured, except where marked] Shapes that only exist under a configuration NEITHER profile pins. Two profiles are now recorded (#357, closing the gap this entry used to only describe): `probes` pins TUI mode, the warm pool and skip-permissions all OFF; `probesTuiPool` turns all three ON (CLAUDE_TUI_MODE=true, OCP_TUI_POOL_SIZE=1, CLAUDE_SKIP_PERMISSIONS=true). Those three are INDEPENDENT — TUI_MODE decides spawn.reason, SKIP_PERMISSIONS decides config.allowedTools[], and tui.pool needs TUI_MODE && OCP_TUI_POOL_SIZE>=1 — so the two corners BRACKET every combination rather than sampling it. That is measured, not argued: the five reachable variants (TUI alone; TUI+pool=1; skip-permissions alone; all three at pool=1; all three at pool=4) were booted against this same fixture and all 16 pairs probed, and NO key path appeared that is absent from both blocks. pool=4 records the same key set as pool=1, because the size is a value. RE-MEASURED AT pool=32 (#404), because `pool=4` was the CAP when this was recorded and therefore read as a boundary measurement; once POOL_MAX_SIZE became 32 it is a mid-range datum at 1/8 of the admissible range, and this entry is PROSPECTIVE — it says what a green run does not cover — so a stale boundary here misleads in the direction of confidence. [measured] Booting this same fixture with OCP_TUI_POOL_SIZE=32 (boot banner `TUI warm pool: ON size=32`) and probing every record gives 200 key paths against the 200 recorded at pool=1, diff empty. [measured] That null is a RESULT and not a vacuous pass, which had to be established rather than assumed: a control compared the same pool=32 probe against the `probes` block, which is known to differ, and the differ reported drift. The first attempt at this measurement printed a bogus total from a WRONG FIELD NAME (`keyPaths` for `keys`) — a differ that reports no difference because it is reading the wrong field is precisely the failure mode this block exists to warn about, so the control is load-bearing here, not ceremony. [measured] Shape-independence was also established from the code itself, separately from the probe above: executing TuiPanePool.stats() at size 1, 4 and 32 returns the SAME 10 keys every time, all of them scalars. [reasoned] The reason it CANNOT vary is visible in the source — stats() returns a fixed object literal of 10 scalar fields with no size-conditional key — so the pool size can only move the VALUE of tui.pool.size and can never add, remove, nest or drop a key. The wire probe, the executed key-set comparison and the structural reading were arrived at separately and agree, which is worth more than any one of them alone. The 12 paths #357 named are now guarded: the 10 tui.pool.* members, plus spawn.reason and config.allowedTools[] which the default block holds. WHAT IS STILL NOT COVERED: any FUTURE setting that decides a response's shape and happens to be pinned to the same value by both profiles. makeB2Fixture's env block comments each pin, and a new shape-deciding setting needs a third profile or a new corner, not a note here.

[measured] The probesTuiPool block records LESS than probes for three endpoints, BY CONSTRUCTION, and a reader must not mistake that for a removal. It runs no warm-up traffic, so /api/usage's byKey[], recent[] and timeline[] and /health's and /status's recentErrors[] are EMPTY arrays there and their ELEMENT keys are absent — 22 + 2 + 2 paths, measured by diffing the two blocks. Every one of those element shapes is recorded in `probes`, so a field added to one is still caught. The reason the warm-up is off is in the next entry.

[measured, except where marked] Neither profile exercises the TUI REQUEST path, so any response surface that appears only after a TUI turn has run is unrecorded. OCP_TUI_TMUX_BIN points at a stub tmux that appends its argv to a log and exits 1, so no pane is ever booted and no `claude` ever runs under tmux; the suite asserts from that log that the only invocation in either profile is `list-sessions`, and that there is exactly one of it under TUI mode. Two things justify the stub, and they were established DIFFERENTLY — which is the point of this tag. [measured] with warm-up traffic under CLAUDE_TUI_MODE=true the two POSTs to /v1/chat/completions issued FOUR `tmux new-session` commands, each launching the configured `claude` binary in a pane; that was observed from the stub's own log. [measured by injection, NOT by observing a real tmux die — and an earlier version of this entry overstated it] server.mjs's boot-time reapStaleTuiSessions({ includeLegacy: true }) can kill-session a live legacy-named `ocp-tui-<8hex>` session, and can reach `tmux kill-server`. Feeding a fake tmux to the REAL reapStaleTuiSessions gives: normal sessions present -> NO kill-server; ONLY a legacy session -> kill-server FIRES; legacy + a normal session -> kill-session fires, kill-server does NOT; another OCP on a different port -> neither; no sessions at all -> kill-server fires with nothing to lose; this instance's OWN port-scoped ocp-tui-<port>-* sessions -> BOTH fire. That last row is the one that makes the gate legible: 'ours' is a SUPERSET of 'legacy-shaped' (isOwn || isLegacyOwn in reapStaleTuiSessions), so othersRemain is about sessions belonging to somebody else, not about session NAME SHAPE. It is unreachable under npm test, which draws a random port, so it is documentation rather than a live hazard. lib/tui/session.mjs's `!othersRemain && sparedLive === 0` gate means ANY ordinary session present stops kill-server, so 'would destroy the operator's whole tmux server on every npm test' was WRONG as written. The mitigation stands on the narrower fact: kill-session on a live legacy-named session is reachable WITH foreign sessions present, and that is someone's running pane.

[reasoned] Responses to a NON-LOCALHOST caller. Probes come from 127.0.0.1, and server.mjs computes 'const isAdmin = AUTH_MODE !== "multi" || authKeyName === "admin" || isLocalhost' (grep that literal; line 3486 as of v3.29.0), so the 401/403 bodies on these endpoints are unreachable from the probe — as is the omission of /health's anonymousKey, guarded by '(isLocalhost || ADVERTISE_ANON_KEY)' (line 3531 as of v3.29.0). Anchored on grep-able literals because bare line numbers in this repo have rotted before; the numbers are secondary and version-pinned. Read from the source, not observed, because the probe has no non-loopback origin available.

[reasoned] ERROR and validation responses. Only the success path of each pair is recorded, by construction of B2_PROBE_PLAN. PATCH /settings's errors[] array exists only when an update is rejected; the 400/404/413 bodies on the key and settings endpoints are likewise absent.

[measured] /status's plan sub-shape. The fixture has no OAuth credentials by construction (otherwise npm test would make a real billed call to api.anthropic.com), and /status returns plan: 'No OAuth token found (keychain / ~/.claude/.credentials.json / CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN)' — a scalar. With live credentials it is an object, and that object's keys are not recorded here.

[measured] /dashboard's body. It is HTML — recorded below as contentType 'text/html' with keys: null, because a key set is not defined for it. RECORDED rather than skipped: status and content-type are still asserted, so if it ever starts returning JSON the test fires.

[reasoned] /usage. It is the Hybrid endpoint (ALIGNMENT.md § Hybrid note), not a row in the B.2 inventory table, and its synthesis layer wraps a live Anthropic wire call that the fixture deliberately cannot make.

[measured] RESOLVED, and kept as a record rather than deleted. This entry used to describe the element keys of sessions[] on /health and /sessions as permanently unrecordable, because nothing in server.mjs ever wrote the sessions Map. Issue #355 / ADR 0016 removed that whole surface instead of leaving it blind: /health.sessions, /health.config.sessionTTL, /status.proxy.activeSessions, /settings.sessionTTL* and both /sessions endpoint records are GONE from the blocks below, so there is no longer an unreachable array here to under-report. The blind spot this entry named was never a gap in the mechanism — the mechanism reported the array accurately; the array was the defect. Recorded because a future reader diffing this file across v3.29.2 will see a large removal and should find its authorization named here as well as in the CHANGELOG.

[measured] Keys of JSON-parseable /logs entries. The fixture seeds one deliberately non-JSON line and the probe records entries[].raw, which is the one part of an entry server.mjs constructs (handleLogs's { raw: line } fallback). A JSON line passes through verbatim, so its keys belong to whatever wrote the log, not to the endpoint, and seeding one would record non-surface as surface.

[measured] REQUEST-SHAPED responses, where the recorded keys are decided by the probe's request body rather than by the server. PATCH /settings echoes one results.<key> sub-object per setting in the body: measured, {timeout} yields results.timeout{,.ok,.value} and {cacheTTL} yields results.cacheTTL{,.ok,.value} — 3 paths swap. The probe therefore pins {timeout} and a change to that body would show as drift with no server change behind it. This is a CATEGORY, not a one-off: B2_PROBE_PLAN already sends all three quota dimensions to PATCH /api/keys/:id/quota for exactly this reason, and the rule was simply not carried across to the adjacent probe until #354's review found it. Anyone adding a probe must ask whether the response echoes the request before choosing a body.
[reasoned] Response HEADERS beyond the content-type family. Only status and content-type are extracted from the response; nothing else is read.

[reasoned] AUTHORIZATION. This says the surface changed. It never says whether the change was allowed. ADR 0012 condition 5 — the marker and the field names in the PR body and the CHANGELOG — is still a human obligation, and this file is the thing that makes forgetting it detectable rather than the thing that satisfies it.

[reasoned] A field that exists ONLY under a new profile's configuration and lands in the SAME PR that introduces that profile. It appears as one of the new block's N key paths, and the `probes` byte-identity check -- the evidence that a new block is coverage rather than surface -- cannot see it, because the field is not reachable under the default configuration at all. So for exactly one PR per profile, 'new coverage' and 'new surface' are indistinguishable to this mechanism. INHERENT to adding a profile rather than introduced by any particular one, and one-time: every later addition to that configuration shows up as a diff inside an existing block, which is fully covered. The controls are the PR narrative and its reviewer, not this file. Named by #382's review and recorded here rather than left for the next profile author to rediscover.
